s: Babylon, Iraq: a complete guide to visiting Nebuchadnezzar's city

Most travellers know Babylon from stories long before they ever see it: the Tower of Babel, the Hanging Gardens, King Nebuchadnezzar, the city where Alexander the Great died. What surprises almost everyone is how easy it is to actually visit Babylon in Iraq today. The ruins lie about 85 km south of Baghdad, and in a single morning you can walk the Processional Way and stand beside brick reliefs of bulls and dragons that were laid more than 2,500 years ago.
This guide covers what to see at Babylon, how to get there from Baghdad, how much time to allow and when to go, with the practical advice I give the travellers I take to the site.
Where is Babylon?

The ruins of Babylon sit in Babil Province in central Iraq, on the banks of the Euphrates and just outside the modern city of Hilla. From Baghdad it is roughly 85 km south, around an hour and a half by car depending on traffic.
In 2019 UNESCO added Babylon to its World Heritage List, recognising a city that for centuries was one of the largest and most influential places in the ancient world. The site is large and open, with original walls, excavated areas and modern reconstructions standing side by side.
A short history of Babylon

Hammurabi and the first great age:
Babylon was already an important town at the start of the second millennium BC, but it became a major capital under Hammurabi, who ruled in the 18th century BC. He is remembered above all for his law code, carved on a black stone stele that is now displayed in the Louvre in Paris.
Nebuchadnezzar II and the city you see today:
Babylon's most famous era came more than a thousand years later, under the Neo-Babylonian kings, and above all Nebuchadnezzar II (reigned 605–562 BC). Most of what visitors see belongs to his building programme: the massive city walls, the royal palaces, the Ishtar Gate and the Processional Way. Many bricks on the site are still stamped with cuneiform inscriptions bearing his name.
Persians, Greeks and a slow fade:
In 539 BC the city passed peacefully to Cyrus the Great of Persia. The famous Cyrus Cylinder, a clay cylinder describing his entry into Babylon, was found here in 1879 and is now in the British Museum in London. In 323 BC Alexander the Great died in Babylon, having planned to make it a capital of his empire. After that the city slowly lost its importance and was eventually abandoned, its mud-brick buildings sinking back into the plain.
What to see at Babylon

The Ishtar Gate and its original reliefs:
The Ishtar Gate was the grand northern entrance to the inner city, dedicated to the goddess Ishtar. Its most spectacular part, covered in blue glazed bricks, was excavated by a German team led by Robert Koldewey in the early 20th century and rebuilt in Berlin's Pergamon Museum. At the entrance to the site you will find a smaller modern replica that gives a sense of the original colours.
The real highlight is less obvious: the original foundations of the gate are still in place. Walk down between the walls and you will see rows of unglazed brick reliefs of bulls and mušḫuššu, the serpent-dragon sacred to the god Marduk, exactly where Nebuchadnezzar's craftsmen set them.
The Processional Way:
From the Ishtar Gate ran the ceremonial road along which statues of the gods were carried during the New Year festival, known as Akitu. Its walls were once lined with glazed lions, the symbol of Ishtar. Today you can walk a section of it and still see stretches of the ancient paving.
The Lion of Babylon:
The most photographed monument on the site is a large basalt lion standing over a human figure. Scholars still debate its date and meaning, but for centuries it has been the emblem of Babylon and one of the best-known images of Iraq.
Nebuchadnezzar's Southern Palace:
The royal palace, with its courtyards and throne room, was largely reconstructed in the 1980s on top of the original foundations. Look closely at the walls and you can tell the ancient bricks, some inscribed, from the modern ones. It is the best place to grasp the sheer scale of the city.
Etemenanki, the "Tower of Babel":
South of the palace stood Etemenanki, the great ziggurat of Marduk, which many historians link to the biblical story of the Tower of Babel. Only the outline of its base survives, and it often holds water after rain. There is little to see, but it is worth pausing to picture a tower that ancient sources describe as around 90 metres high.
The Hanging Gardens: legend or reality?:
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon are one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, yet no firm archaeological evidence for them has been found at Babylon. Some scholars suggest they may have stood in another city, possibly Nineveh. Local guides point out a few candidate spots near the palace; it makes for a good conversation on site, as long as you know the debate is still open.
How to get to Babylon from Baghdad

There is no convenient public transport for tourists to the site itself, so the easiest options are a private car with a driver or an organised tour. The drive from Baghdad takes about an hour and a half. You will pass through several routine checkpoints along the way, which are normal in Iraq; keep your passport within reach.
Travelling with a local guide makes the day simpler: tickets, checkpoints and timing are taken care of, and you arrive in the best light of the day.
Best time to visit Babylon

The ideal season runs from October to April, when days are mild and sunny. From June to September temperatures often pass 45 °C and walking around an open site becomes tiring, so if you travel in summer, arrive early in the morning.
Allow two to three hours on site. A day trip from Baghdad is the most common way to visit, and it leaves time to return to the capital for dinner, or to continue south towards Karbala and Najaf.
Practical tips for your visit

• Tickets: bought at the site entrance. Prices can change, so carry enough cash in Iraqi dinars.
• What to wear: comfortable shoes, a hat and water, even in spring. Modest clothing (shoulders and knees covered) is always appreciated.
• Photography: generally allowed across the site. Morning light is best for the reliefs of the Ishtar Gate foundations.
• Visa: entry rules for Iraq change from time to time, so always check the latest official information for your nationality before you book.
• Bring a guide: there are few information panels on site, and without someone to explain each wall, many details are easy to miss.
Babylon on an Iraq itinerary

Babylon pairs naturally with the other highlights of central and southern Iraq: the shrine cities of Karbala and Najaf, the Sumerian cities of Uruk and Ur, and the Mesopotamian Marshes. On our 7-day Iraq heritage tour, Babylon is one of the first stops after Baghdad, and it is often the moment when travellers really understand why Iraq is called the cradle of civilisation. If you have more time, the 9-day tour adds the north as well.
When I walk a group along the Processional Way, I always ask them to touch one of the original bricks. Knowing it was laid in the time of Nebuchadnezzar changes the way you look at the whole city. — Saif

s: The Imam Ali Shrine in Najaf: history, what to see and how to visit

Few places in Iraq leave as deep an impression as the Imam Ali Shrine in Najaf. Rising above the old city, its golden dome and twin gilded minarets catch the desert light from far away, and day and night the courtyards are full of pilgrims who have travelled from across Iraq and the wider world. If you are planning to visit Najaf, this guide explains the shrine's history, what you will see inside the complex, how to get there from Baghdad and the etiquette that makes a visit go smoothly.
For Shia Muslims this is one of the holiest places on earth, the resting place of Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him), cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad. For travellers of every background it is also one of the great monuments of Islamic architecture, shaped over more than a thousand years by Abbasid, Buyid, Safavid and later patrons.
Where is the Imam Ali Shrine?

The shrine stands at the heart of Najaf, a city on the edge of the western desert, roughly 160 km south of Baghdad. The drive usually takes around two and a half to three hours. Najaf also has its own international airport, which receives flights from several countries in the region.
Just 10 km away lies Kufa, the city Imam Ali made his capital, and on the northern edge of Najaf stretches Wadi al-Salam, the "Valley of Peace", one of the largest cemeteries in the world. Together, Najaf and Kufa form one of the most meaningful days of any heritage journey through Iraq.
The history of the shrine

A hidden grave:
Imam Ali was struck while leading the dawn prayer in the Great Mosque of Kufa during Ramadan and passed away a few days later, in the year 40 AH (661 CE). According to tradition, his family buried him at night, outside the city and in secret, so that the grave would be protected. For more than a century its location was known only to his descendants and a small circle of followers.
The gazelle of Harun al-Rashid:
A well-known story tells how the grave came to light. The Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid was hunting near Kufa when a gazelle took refuge on a small rise; his hounds and falcons refused to follow it there. When the caliph asked about the place, he was told it was the grave of Ali ibn Abi Talib. Around 786 CE he ordered the first building over the tomb, a modest structure with a dome and four entrances.
Buyids, Safavids and the golden dome:
In the late 10th century the Buyid ruler 'Adud al-Dawla built a far grander shrine and endowed the growing town around it; he himself chose to be buried inside the complex. The famous Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta, who came in 1327, described silk carpets and lamps of gold and silver.
The shrine you see today largely takes its form from the Safavid period in the 17th century, when the great courtyard was laid out according to a design attributed to the scholar and architect Sheikh Baha'i. In 1743 Nader Shah ordered the dome and minarets to be covered in gilded copper plates, replacing the earlier blue and green tiles, and creating the golden silhouette that has become the symbol of Najaf.
What to see inside the complex

The great courtyard:
The shrine sits in the middle of a vast open courtyard framed by two storeys of pointed arches, faced with blue, turquoise and yellow tilework. In past centuries the small rooms behind these arches housed students of Najaf's religious seminary, one of the oldest centres of learning in the Islamic world. In the evening, when the lights come on and families sit on carpets in the courtyard, the atmosphere is calm and unforgettable.
The Clock Gate and the other portals:
Most visitors enter from the east through the Clock Gate, crowned by a tiled clock tower. Its clock and bells were made in Manchester, England, and installed in 1887 — a surprising detail for British visitors. Other entrances carry the names of the scholar Sheikh al-Tusi and of Muslim ibn Aqil, the cousin of Imam Hussein.
The Golden Iwan:
Facing the courtyard on the east side of the sanctuary is the Golden Iwan, a monumental open hall entirely covered in gold and flanked by the two gilded minarets. Persian verses praising Imam Ali were inscribed here in gold in the 18th century.
The sanctuary:
Inside, the tomb chamber glitters with thousands of pieces of mirror mosaic that reflect the light of the chandeliers. The tomb itself is enclosed in a richly worked silver screen, called a zarih, crafted by Indian artisans and unveiled in 1942. According to Shia tradition, the Prophets Adam and Noah are also buried here, beside Imam Ali.
How to get to Najaf from Baghdad

Most travellers reach Najaf by road from Baghdad, often combining the journey with Babylon or Karbala. A private car with driver is the most comfortable option, as it lets you stop on the way and arrive at the shrine at a good time of day. If your trip starts in the south, Najaf's airport is a practical alternative. From the city centre, the shrine is reached on foot through the old covered market, which leads straight to the eastern gate.
Best time to visit

The most comfortable months are October to April, when the days are warm but not hot. Summer in Najaf is very hot, so plan visits for early morning or after sunset. Evenings are particularly beautiful: the dome glows in the floodlights and the courtyards are at their liveliest.
Major religious anniversaries draw very large crowds. They are deeply moving to witness, but if you prefer a quieter visit, ask your guide about the calendar before fixing your dates.
Practical tips and etiquette

• Dress modestly: men in long trousers and sleeves; women cover their hair and wear a long, loose robe (abaya). Your guide can help you arrange one.
• Shoes: you leave them at the shoe depositories near the entrances before stepping into the courtyard and collect them with a token on the way out.
• Security: there are bag checks at the gates. Travel light and leave large bags in the car or hotel.
• Photography: rules can change; phones are usually fine in the courtyards, but always ask before photographing people, and be discreet inside the sanctuary.
• Non-Muslim visitors: respectful visitors are welcomed in the courtyards, and going with a local guide makes everything easier.
• Visa and entry: rules change from time to time, so check the current requirements for your nationality before you travel.
"I always try to bring my guests to the shrine in the hour before sunset. You see the gold turn warm in the evening light, then the lamps come on and the whole courtyard changes. Afterwards we walk through the old market for tea — it is the best way to feel Najaf." — Saif
The Imam Ali Shrine in an Iraq itinerary

Najaf fits naturally into a journey through central and southern Iraq. On our 7-day Iraq heritage tour it is combined with Kufa and Karbala, after a day among the ruins of ancient Babylon. Travellers who want more time in the south can choose the 9-day itinerary, which continues towards Basra, the Marshes and the ziggurat of Ur.
Whatever your reason for coming — faith, history or simple curiosity — an evening in the courtyard of the Imam Ali Shrine is one of those moments that stay with you long after you leave Iraq.

s: The Imam Hussein Shrine in Karbala: history, what to see and how to visit

Arriving at the Imam Hussein Shrine in Karbala is an experience that few travellers forget. A golden dome rises above the rooftops, two gilded minarets frame it against the sky, and from early morning until long after midnight a steady stream of visitors flows through its gates. If you plan to visit Karbala in Iraq, this guide covers the shrine's story, what to look for inside the complex, how to get there from Baghdad and the etiquette that makes a visit easy and respectful.
For Shia Muslims the shrine is among the most sacred places in the world: it holds the tomb of Imam Hussein ibn Ali (peace be upon him), grandson of the Prophet Muhammad and son of Imam Ali and Fatima al-Zahra. For travellers of any faith, it is also a remarkable piece of Islamic architecture and the beating heart of a city whose whole identity grew up around a single grave.
Where is the Imam Hussein Shrine?

The shrine stands in the centre of Karbala, a city on the edge of the desert west of the Euphrates, roughly 100 km south-west of Baghdad. By car the journey usually takes around one and a half to two hours, depending on traffic and checkpoints. Najaf is about 80 km further south, and the ruins of Babylon lie a short drive to the east, so Karbala sits right at the centre of Iraq's classic heritage route.
A few hundred metres to the north-east rises a second golden dome: the shrine of al-Abbas, Imam Hussein's half-brother. The wide pedestrian esplanade that links the two sanctuaries is called Bayn al-Haramayn, "between the two shrines", and walking it is one of the defining moments of any visit to Karbala.
A short history of the shrine

Karbala in 680 CE:
In the year 61 AH (680 CE), Imam Hussein travelled from Medina towards Kufa with members of his family and a small group of companions. On the plain of Karbala, beside the Euphrates, they were stopped by a much larger army. On the tenth day of the month of Muharram, the day known as Ashura, Imam Hussein and his companions were killed. For Muslims, and above all for Shia Muslims, his stand has become a timeless symbol of principle, sacrifice and refusal to accept injustice. He was buried where he fell, and the place soon became a destination for visitors.
The first buildings:
According to tradition, the first structure over the grave was a simple building of brick and plaster, raised by local people of the Banu Asad tribe or in the time of al-Mukhtar al-Thaqafi a few years after the battle. Under the early Abbasids a dome and gates were added, and the shrine was rebuilt and extended several times over the following centuries.
From the Buyids to the Qajars:
A decisive phase came in the late 10th century, when the Buyid ruler 'Adud al-Dawla carried out a major building programme between about 977 and 982 CE. The dome he raised over the tomb forms the core of the sanctuary you see today. In the 14th century the Jalayirid rulers completed the Golden Iwan, the great open hall facing the courtyard. Safavid patrons later added a new screen around the tomb and a carved wooden sarcophagus.
The golden look of Karbala belongs largely to the Qajar era. In the 1790s Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar ordered the dome to be rebuilt and covered in gold, and his successor Fath-Ali Shah commissioned a new tomb screen. Gilding of the iwan and minarets followed, and the dome was regilded several times in later generations.
What to see inside the complex

The golden dome and minarets:
The outer dome rises about 27 metres and is entirely sheathed in gold, with a ring of twelve windows around its base. Flanked by its two gilded minarets, it glows warm amber in the late afternoon and shines brilliantly under the floodlights at night — the moment most photographers wait for.
The courtyard and the gates:
The shrine is enclosed by a wall pierced by ten gates, their wooden doors decorated with glass and tilework. Behind them, two storeys of arched rooms line a broad courtyard; for centuries these rooms housed students and scholars. The best-known entrance is the Qibla Gate, also called the Golden Gate (Bab al-Dhahab). Look up at the tile panels above the arches: deep blues, turquoise and saffron yellow, with Qur'anic verses and floral patterns that change with the light.
The sanctuary and the zarih:
Inside the sanctuary, walls and ceilings sparkle with mirror mosaic that multiplies the light of the chandeliers. The tomb itself is enclosed in a zarih, a richly worked screen of silver and gold. The current one was crafted in Qom from gold, silver, copper, brass and teak, and was unveiled in 2013 after years of work by master craftsmen.
Those buried beside the Imam:
Imam Hussein does not rest alone. According to tradition, his son Ali al-Akbar is buried at his feet, and the companions who fell with him lie together nearby within the sanctuary. Close to the entrance is the tomb of Habib ibn Mazahir al-Asadi, an elderly companion of the Imam who is especially loved by visitors.
Bayn al-Haramayn and the shrine of al-Abbas

Leaving the shrine through its north-eastern gates you step onto Bayn al-Haramayn, the open, paved promenade that leads to the shrine of al-Abbas ibn Ali. Al-Abbas was Imam Hussein's half-brother and standard-bearer, remembered for his loyalty and courage. Walking slowly between the two golden domes, especially in the evening when families stroll and the lights come on, is one of the most memorable things you can do in Iraq. Allow time for both sanctuaries: they are part of the same visit and form a single spiritual landscape.
How to get to Karbala from Baghdad

Most travellers reach Karbala by road from Baghdad. A private car with driver is the most comfortable option, since it lets you combine Karbala with Babylon the same day or continue on to Najaf. Visitors coming from the south can also use Najaf's international airport, about an hour and a half away by road. Near the shrines, the streets are largely pedestrian, so expect to walk the last part on foot through the busy market streets — which is part of the charm.
Best time to visit

The most pleasant months are October to April, when days are warm and evenings mild. Summer temperatures are very high, so plan visits for early morning or after sunset. Whatever the season, the hour before sunset and the evening are the best times: the gold turns soft, the courtyards fill with families and the atmosphere becomes calm and intimate.
Karbala hosts some of the largest religious gatherings in the world, above all during Muharram and on Arbaeen, forty days after Ashura, when millions of pilgrims arrive — many on foot from Najaf and other cities. Witnessing these days is deeply moving, but the city is extremely crowded. If you prefer a quieter visit, ask your guide about the calendar before setting your dates.
Practical tips and etiquette

• Dress modestly: men wear long trousers and sleeves; women cover their hair and wear a long, loose abaya. Your guide can help you arrange one.
• Shoes: leave them at the shoe depositories by the gates and collect them with your token when you leave.
• Security checks: bags are checked at the entrances to the shrine area. Travel light and leave large bags in the car or hotel.
• Photography: rules can change; phones are usually fine in the courtyards and on Bayn al-Haramayn, but always ask before photographing people, and be discreet inside the sanctuary.
• Non-Muslim visitors: respectful visitors are welcomed in the courtyards, and going with a local guide makes entrances and customs easier to navigate.
• Visa and entry: requirements change from time to time, so check the current rules for your nationality before you travel.
"When I bring guests to Karbala, I like to arrive in the late afternoon. We visit the shrine of Imam Hussein first, then walk across Bayn al-Haramayn to al-Abbas just as the lights come on. Many of my guests tell me that walk was the moment they will remember most from Iraq." — Saif
The Imam Hussein Shrine in an Iraq itinerary

Karbala fits naturally into a journey through central Iraq. On our 7-day Iraq heritage tour it sits between the ancient ruins of Babylon and the golden dome of the Imam Ali Shrine in Najaf, together with Kufa. Travellers who want more time in the south can choose the 9-day itinerary, continuing to Ur, the Marshes and Basra.
Whether you come as a pilgrim, a lover of history or simply a curious traveller, an evening between the two golden shrines of Karbala is one of those experiences that stays with you long after your journey ends.

s: The Ishtar Gate of Babylon: history and what you can still see in Iraq

Few monuments of the ancient world are as instantly recognisable as the Ishtar Gate of Babylon: a wall of deep blue glazed bricks, crossed by rows of golden bulls and strange serpent-dragons. Most people have seen it in photographs from a museum in Berlin. Far fewer know that you can still stand at the place where it was built, in Babylon in central Iraq, and see parts of the original gate that never left the ground.
This guide explains what the Ishtar Gate was, what happened to it, what you can see of it at Babylon today and how to fit a visit into a trip to Iraq, with the tips I share with the travellers I bring to the site.
What was the Ishtar Gate of Babylon?

The Ishtar Gate was the grand northern entrance to the inner city of Babylon. It was built around 575 BC on the orders of Nebuchadnezzar II, the king who turned Babylon into one of the largest and most splendid cities of its time. The inner city had eight gates, each named after a god, and this one was dedicated to Ishtar, the goddess of love and war.
It was not only a doorway. The gate was a statement of power and faith, the first thing a visitor, an ambassador or a religious procession would see when entering the heart of the capital. Through it passed the Processional Way, the sacred road that led towards the temple of Marduk, the chief god of Babylon.
Bulls, dragons and lions: reading the walls

What makes the Ishtar Gate unforgettable is its decoration. The walls were faced with bricks covered in a shining blue glaze, a colour that recalled precious lapis lazuli. On this blue background, craftsmen set animals moulded in relief and glazed in yellow, brown and white, arranged in long alternating rows.
The bull of Adad:
The bulls, often described as aurochs, a wild ox now extinct, were the animal of Adad, the god of storms and rain. In a land that lived from its rivers and its harvests, he was a god people took very seriously.
The mušḫuššu of Marduk:
The second animal is the most striking: the mušḫuššu, a creature with a scaly body, a serpent's head and tongue, the front legs of a lion and the back legs of a bird of prey. It was the sacred beast of Marduk. Children who visit Babylon usually call it "the dragon", and that is not far from the truth.
The lions of Ishtar:
Along the walls of the Processional Way, leading up to the gate, walked rows of glazed lions, the symbol of Ishtar herself. Together, bulls, dragons and lions formed a kind of guard of honour of the gods for everyone who entered the city.
Nebuchadnezzar also left a long cuneiform inscription describing the work. In it, the king explains that he rebuilt the gate, decorated it with blue bricks and figures of bulls and dragons, and roofed it with cedar, so that people would gaze at it in wonder. Nearly 2,600 years later, they still do.
From Babylon to Berlin: the gate's journey

For centuries the gate lay buried under the ruins of Babylon. Between 1902 and 1914 a German expedition led by the architect and archaeologist Robert Koldewey excavated the area and recovered a huge number of glazed brick fragments. These were shipped to Germany, sorted and pieced together over many years.
The result is the famous reconstruction in Berlin's Pergamon Museum, unveiled in 1930, which shows the smaller front section of the gate together with part of the Processional Way. The museum has been closed for a long renovation, with a phased reopening announced, so check its official website before planning a visit. Single panels of lions, bulls and dragons are also displayed in several other museums around the world, including in Istanbul, Paris and New York.
What you can see of the Ishtar Gate in Babylon today

The blue replica at the entrance:
When you arrive at the archaeological site of Babylon, near the city of Hilla, the first thing you notice is a bright blue gate with rows of animals: a smaller modern replica of the Ishtar Gate. It is not ancient, but it is perfect for understanding the colours and the rhythm of the original decoration, and on a sunny day, with the blue sky behind it, it is one of the most photographed spots in Iraq.
The original foundations, still in place:
The real treasure lies a little further on. The gate was rebuilt and raised several times, and its lower levels, made of unglazed bricks, stayed underground when the upper parts were taken away. Today you can walk down between these original walls and see dozens of bulls and dragons in relief, standing exactly where Nebuchadnezzar's builders placed them. They are the colour of earth rather than blue, but touching them is a direct link to the Babylon of the 6th century BC.
The Processional Way:
From the gate you can follow part of the Processional Way, the road along which the statues of the gods were carried during the New Year festival, the Akitu. Imagining the music, the crowds and the glazed lions on both sides is easy once you stand there.
For the rest of the site, including the Lion of Babylon, the Southern Palace and the base of the great ziggurat, see my complete guide to visiting Babylon.
How to get to the Ishtar Gate from Baghdad

Babylon lies about 85 km south of Baghdad, roughly an hour and a half by car depending on traffic. There is no practical public transport for tourists to the site, so most visitors come by private car with a driver or on an organised tour. On the way you will pass routine checkpoints; keep your passport at hand.
The Ishtar Gate area is right at the start of the visit, so it is the natural first stop before you continue into the rest of the ruins.
Best time to visit

The most comfortable months are October to April, when days are mild and the light is soft. In summer temperatures often climb above 45 °C, so if you travel then, arrive as early as possible. For photographs, the morning sun lights the blue replica beautifully, while the reliefs in the original foundations show their details best when the sun is not straight overhead.
Allow at least an hour for the gate, the foundations and the Processional Way, and two to three hours for the whole of Babylon.
Practical tips

• Tickets: sold at the site entrance. Prices can change, so carry some cash in Iraqi dinars.
• Shoes and sun: the ground is uneven and there is little shade. Bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
• Look down, not only up: many visitors photograph the blue replica and leave. The original reliefs in the foundations are the part you will remember.
• Before or after Berlin: if you have seen the reconstruction in Berlin, Babylon shows you its original setting; if you visit Babylon first, Berlin will feel like meeting an old friend.
• Visa: entry rules for Iraq change from time to time, so check the latest official information for your nationality before booking.
The Ishtar Gate on an Iraq itinerary

A visit to the Ishtar Gate fits naturally into a day in Babylon, which can be combined with the shrine cities of Karbala and Najaf further south. On our 7-day Iraq heritage tour Babylon comes early in the trip, right after Baghdad, and it is often where travellers first feel the depth of Mesopotamian history. After Babylon, many continue to Najaf to visit the Imam Ali Shrine. The 9-day tour adds the north as well.
At the gate I always stop the group in front of one particular dragon in the foundations. Its tongue, its claws, even the curl of its tail are still sharp after more than two and a half thousand years. That is the moment people stop taking photos and just look. — Saif

q: Where is Al-Mutanabbi Street?
In the old city of Baghdad, on the Rusafa side on the east bank of the Tigris. It branches off al-Rasheed Street and ends at the river.
When is the best time to visit Mutanabbi Street?
Friday morning, when second-hand books cover the pavements and the street is buzzing. The cooler months from October to April are the most pleasant.
Who was al-Mutanabbi?
Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi was an Abbasid-era poet, born around 915 in Kufa and died in 965, regarded as one of the greatest poets of the Arabic language.
What is Shabandar Café?
A legendary tea house from 1917 at the end of the street, a meeting place for writers and intellectuals, its walls covered with old photographs.
What else is nearby?
The Qishla and its clock tower, Souq al-Saray, al-Mustansiriya Madrasa, the Baghdadi Museum and the coppersmiths' Souq al-Safafeer are all within walking distance.
Is Mutanabbi Street part of the tour?
Yes, it is part of the Baghdad day on Fable Tour's 7-day Iraq tour, usually with tea at Shabandar Café.
s: Al-Mutanabbi Street in Baghdad: the book street, Friday market and Shabandar Café

If you love bookshops, Al-Mutanabbi Street in Baghdad will feel like coming home. This narrow, car-free lane in the old heart of the city has been the place where Iraqis buy, sell, swap and argue about books for generations. On Friday mornings it turns into a great open-air book market, and you suddenly understand why Baghdad is known as a city that reads.
In this guide you will find where Mutanabbi Street is, the poet behind its name, what to see on the way down to the Tigris and how to get the most out of your visit, with tips from Saif, your local guide in Baghdad.
Where is Al-Mutanabbi Street in Baghdad?

Al-Mutanabbi Street lies on the Rusafa side of Baghdad, the east bank of the Tigris, right in the historic centre. It is a narrow pedestrian street, just under a kilometre long, that branches off al-Rasheed Street, the old main avenue of Baghdad, and runs down towards the river, ending in a small square with a view over the water.
That location makes it the perfect starting point for exploring old Baghdad on foot. Several of the city's most interesting historic places are within a few minutes' walk, so you can easily spend a whole morning here without getting into a car.
The history of Baghdad's book street

An Abbasid inheritance:
According to tradition, the book trade in this quarter goes back to the Abbasid era, when Baghdad was one of the world's great centres of learning. It was the age of the House of Wisdom, of translators and copyists, and of the warraqin, the paper-makers and book-sellers who produced and sold handwritten volumes. Walking between the stalls today, it is easy to imagine that long line running from then to now.
The poet behind the name:
The street received its present name in 1932, under King Faisal I, in honour of the poet Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi. Born around 915 in Kufa and died in 965, he is considered one of the greatest poets in the history of the Arabic language. His verses are famous for their pride and sharp wit, and many of his lines have become sayings that Iraqis still quote every day. It says a lot about Baghdad that its book street carries his name.
"Cairo writes, Beirut prints, Baghdad reads":
A well-known saying in the Arab world divides the roles this way. It is meant with a smile, but on Mutanabbi Street it rings true. Here reading is not a solitary hobby; it is something people share, discuss and celebrate together.
What to see on Mutanabbi Street

The entrance arch and the bookshops:
You enter through an arch decorated with lines from the poet's work. Beyond it, bookshops, stationers, printers and second-hand stalls line both sides of the street. You will find school books and dictionaries, poetry, history, philosophy and old magazines. The street has been renovated in recent years, with new stone paving, lighting and restored façades, and it is now a real pleasure to stroll.
The Friday book market:
The highlight is Friday morning. Second-hand books are spread out on the pavements and the street fills with families, students, poets, artists and musicians. People read aloud, debate and strike up conversations over piles of books. The atmosphere feels more like a cultural festival than a market.
The statue of al-Mutanabbi:
At the end of the street stands a bronze statue of the poet, made in 1977 by the Iraqi sculptor Mohammed Ghani Hikmat. It overlooks the Tigris from a small square and is one of the most photographed spots in old Baghdad, especially under a deep blue sky with the clock tower of the Qishla behind it.
Shabandar Café and the Qishla

A tea house for writers:
Near the bottom of the street, close to the Qishla, is Shabandar Café, founded in 1917. It is a legendary meeting place for writers and intellectuals, its walls covered with old black-and-white photographs of Baghdad. Order strong tea in a small istikan glass and sit among the regulars: there are few better ways to feel the city's cultural life.
The Qishla by the river:
The Qishla is an Ottoman-era government building from the second half of the 19th century, with a clock tower about 22 metres high. Today it is a cultural space with gardens that reach down to the Tigris, a lovely place to rest in the shade after browsing.
Nearby sights in old Baghdad

Mutanabbi Street combines easily with other places in the old city, all within walking distance:
Souq al-Saray:
Right next to the street is Souq al-Saray, an old market of around 300 metres selling stationery and books, entered near the al-Saray Mosque, built in 1660.
Al-Mustansiriya Madrasa:
Founded by the caliph al-Mustansir in the 1220s–1230s, this Abbasid school is considered one of the oldest universities in the world and is the natural next stop for anyone fascinated by the history of learning.
The Baghdadi Museum and Souq al-Safafeer:
The Baghdadi Museum recreates traditional city life, while Souq al-Safafeer, the coppersmiths' market, is known for the sound of hammers on metal.
Best time to visit the Baghdad book market

Friday morning is without doubt the best time, when the street is at its liveliest and the famous book market is in full swing. On other days it is quieter, which can be nice if you want to browse at leisure. For the season, the cooler months from October to April are the most pleasant for exploring the city on foot.
Practical tips for your visit

• Arrive early on Friday to see the market before it gets really busy.
• Bring cash in small notes; it makes buying from the stalls much easier.
• Wear comfortable shoes: the street is pedestrian and you will walk a lot in the old city.
• Ask before photographing people; most are friendly, but it is polite.
• Dress neatly and modestly, with shoulders and knees covered, as elsewhere in Baghdad.
• Leave time for a glass of tea at Shabandar Café; it is part of the experience.
• Entry rules for Iraq change from time to time, so check the latest official visa information before booking.
Friday morning is my favourite moment in Baghdad. I take my guests to Mutanabbi Street while the books are still being laid out on the pavement, and we always finish with tea at Shabandar. That is where you see the city the way we who live here know it. — Saif
Mutanabbi Street on an Iraq tour

A visit to Mutanabbi Street is part of the Baghdad day on our 7-day Iraq tour, when we explore the old city on foot, including the book street, the Qishla and the banks of the Tigris. The same journey takes you south to ancient Babylon and to the holy cities, including the Imam Ali Shrine in Najaf. Together, these places show an Iraq that is both the cradle of civilisation and a living land of culture, where books, poetry and conversation still sit at the centre of life.

q: Where is the Great Mosque of Kufa?
In the old centre of Kufa, on the Euphrates, about 10 km northeast of Najaf in southern-central Iraq.
Why is the Kufa mosque important?
It is one of the oldest mosques in the world and the place where Imam Ali led prayers, preached and judged while Kufa was his capital.
What are the maqams in the courtyard?
Small covered platforms marking places linked by tradition to prophets and Imams, such as Abraham, Adam, Gabriel and Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq.
Can non-Muslims visit the Great Mosque of Kufa?
Respectful visitors are generally welcomed in the courtyard with modest dress; women are usually asked to wear an abaya. Follow the guidance of the staff.
How long does a visit take?
Allow 1.5 to 2 hours including the nearby House of Imam Ali and the shrine of Muslim ibn Aqil.
Do I need a visa to visit Iraq?
Entry rules change from time to time. Check the latest official information for your nationality before booking your trip.
s: The Great Mosque of Kufa: history, holy stations and how to visit

A short drive from the golden dome of Najaf, the Great Mosque of Kufa rises behind tall, honey-coloured walls. It is one of the oldest mosques in the world, the place where Imam Ali (peace be upon him) prayed, taught and judged during his years in Kufa, and today one of the most visited stops for travellers and pilgrims in southern Iraq. If you plan to visit the Great Mosque of Kufa, this guide explains its history, what to look for inside and how to fit it into an Iraq itinerary.
I bring guests here on almost every trip through the holy cities. Many expect "just another mosque" and leave saying it was the calmest, most moving hour of their journey. Here is why.
Where is the Great Mosque of Kufa?

Kufa lies on the Euphrates in central-southern Iraq, about 10 km northeast of Najaf, in Najaf Province. Today the two cities have almost grown into one another, so the mosque is usually visited on the same day as the Imam Ali Shrine in Najaf. From Baghdad the drive south takes roughly three hours, depending on traffic and checkpoints, and Karbala is about an hour and a half away by road.
The mosque stands in the old heart of Kufa. Around it you will find several smaller shrines and historic houses that belong to the same story, which makes the area perfect to explore on foot.
A short history of one of the oldest mosques in the world

A new city on the Euphrates:
Kufa was founded around 638 CE, in the first decades of Islam, as a new settlement on the edge of the desert. According to the historical sources, the mosque was laid out at the same time as the city, under Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, with the governor's palace, the Dar al-Imara, built right next to it. At first it was a simple open space marked out on the ground; around 670 CE the governor Ziyad rebuilt it in brick and enlarged it, bringing columns from far away.
Older than history, according to tradition:
Muslim tradition gives the site a much longer story. Several narrations say that a place of prayer stood here since the time of Prophet Adam, and that Prophet Noah lived nearby and built his ark on this ground. That is why visitors find stations inside the mosque linked to Noah, Abraham and other prophets. Whether you read these traditions as history or as faith, they explain why so many people feel the place is special.
The capital of Imam Ali:
The mosque's most important chapter began in 656 CE, when Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib made Kufa the centre of his caliphate. He led prayers in this mosque, gave sermons from it, and sat in judgement among the people. His words on justice, piety and good government, later collected in the famous book Nahj al-Balagha, were delivered in large part in Kufa. In Ramadan of the year 40 AH (early 661 CE), the Imam was struck while leading the dawn prayer in this mosque and passed away two days later. His burial place is in Najaf, where his great shrine stands today.
Later centuries:
Kufa remained a great centre of learning for centuries, famous for its grammarians, Qur'an reciters and its angular Kufic script, which takes its name from the city. The mosque was restored many times. The golden dome above the tombs and much of the tilework date to later periods, and the most recent large renovation, completed around 2010, gave the courtyard its gleaming white marble and decorated the prayer halls richly.
What to see inside the Great Mosque of Kufa

The walls and the great courtyard:
From outside, the mosque looks almost like a fortress: a nearly square enclosure, around 110 metres on each side, with high walls, round towers and four minarets. Step through the gate and the space opens into a huge, bright courtyard. On a clear evening the marble reflects the sky, and the golden dome and minarets glow in the last light. This is one of the most beautiful sights of any trip to Iraq.
The maqams: stations of prophets and Imams:
Scattered across the courtyard are small, covered platforms called maqams, each marking a place connected by tradition to a prophet or an Imam. Among them are the stations of Prophet Abraham, of Prophet Adam, of the angel Gabriel, of Imam Zayn al-Abidin and of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq. Pilgrims move from one to the next, praying a few moments at each. As a visitor, you are welcome to walk around quietly and watch this gentle rhythm.
The place of Noah's Ark:
One corner of the courtyard is linked by tradition to Noah: the place where, it is said, the waters of the flood began and where the ark came to rest. It is a striking spot to hear the story told in the very place it is remembered.
The Dakkat al-Qada and the mihrab of Imam Ali:
The Dakkat al-Qada, the "bench of judgement", marks where Imam Ali is said to have heard cases and settled disputes; it is a reminder of his reputation for fairness. Inside the prayer hall, the mihrab where he was leading the prayer when he was struck is the emotional heart of the mosque. Visitors stand here in silence, and many recite prayers for him.
The shrines of Muslim ibn Aqil and Hani ibn Urwa:
Attached to the mosque are the domed shrines of Muslim ibn Aqil, the cousin and envoy of Imam Hussein, and of Hani ibn Urwa, the Kufan nobleman who hosted him. Nearby lies the tomb of al-Mukhtar al-Thaqafi. These shrines connect Kufa with the story of Karbala, which many travellers visit next.
Around the mosque: the House of Imam Ali

A few minutes' walk away is the modest house where, according to tradition, Imam Ali lived with his family while in Kufa. Its simplicity, with small rooms and an old well, contrasts strongly with the grandeur of the mosque, and many visitors find it the most touching stop of the day. Close by you can also see the remains of the Dar al-Imara, the governor's palace excavated by archaeologists, and the shrine of Maytham al-Tammar, a companion of Imam Ali. A little outside the centre stands Masjid al-Sahla, another historic mosque of Kufa.
How to get to Kufa

Most travellers reach Kufa from Najaf, which has an international airport and plenty of hotels. A taxi or private car from the Imam Ali Shrine takes about 15–20 minutes. Coming from Baghdad, the road goes south via Hilla, which allows a stop at ancient Babylon on the way. On a guided tour, Kufa, Najaf and Karbala are usually combined over one or two days.
Best time to visit

The most pleasant months are October to April, when days are mild and evenings are cool. The late afternoon is magical: the heat eases, the courtyard fills with families and the marble turns gold at sunset. In summer, plan your visit for early morning or after sunset. Be aware that during major religious occasions Kufa and Najaf receive very large crowds; this can be a powerful experience, but you should plan accommodation well ahead.
Practical tips for visiting the Great Mosque of Kufa

• Dress modestly: men in long trousers and sleeves; women cover hair, arms and legs. Women are usually asked to wear an abaya, and one can often be borrowed near the entrance.
• Shoes are left at a shoe depository at the gate; keep your token safe.
• Bags may be checked at the entrance, so travel light.
• Photography of the courtyard is generally fine, but be discreet and do not photograph people praying without permission.
• Walk on the left of praying people, never directly in front of them.
• Combine the mosque with the House of Imam Ali nearby; allow at least 1.5–2 hours in total.
• Entry rules for Iraq change from time to time, so check the latest official visa information for your nationality before booking.
When guests ask me where they felt Iraq's history most strongly, many answer: sitting in the courtyard of Kufa at sunset, hearing the call to prayer and realising that Imam Ali walked on this same ground fourteen centuries ago. — Saif
Kufa in an Iraq heritage trip

The Great Mosque of Kufa is part of our 7-day Iraq heritage tour, on the day dedicated to Kufa and Najaf, and it also appears in the 9-day itinerary. Together with the shrine of Imam Ali in Najaf and the Imam Hussein Shrine in Karbala, it completes a journey through the places that shaped early Islamic history, and it shows a side of Iraq that is warm, welcoming and deeply spiritual.

q: Where is the Ziggurat of Ur?
At Tell al-Muqayyar in Dhi Qar province, southern Iraq, about 15 km southwest of Nasiriyah and west of the Euphrates.
Who built the Ziggurat of Ur?
King Ur-Nammu, founder of the Third Dynasty of Ur, began it around 2100 BC; his son Shulgi completed it. Nabonidus of Babylon restored it in the 6th century BC.
What was the ziggurat used for?
It was a stepped temple platform with a shrine on top, dedicated to Nanna, the moon god and patron of Ur. It was not a tomb.
Is Ur really the city of Abraham?
According to tradition, Ur of the Chaldees was the birthplace of the Prophet Abraham, and a restored house in the old quarter is known as the House of Abraham.
How do I get to Ur from Baghdad?
Nasiriyah is around 360 km south of Baghdad, roughly five hours by road, and the site is a short drive from there. Most visitors combine Ur with the Marshes and Basra.
When is the best time to visit Ur?
From October to April. Come early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light is soft and the bricks glow gold.
s: The Great Ziggurat of Ur: history, what to see and how to visit

Long before pyramids rose on the Nile, the Sumerians of southern Mesopotamia were stacking millions of bricks into stepped temple mountains. The finest one still standing is the Great Ziggurat of Ur, near Nasiriyah in southern Iraq. Visiting the Ziggurat of Ur means walking up to a monument more than 4,000 years old, in the city that the Bible remembers as Ur of the Chaldees, the hometown of Abraham.
In this guide you will learn where the ziggurat is, who built it and why, what else to see in ancient Ur, and how to fit it into your journey through Iraq, with the tips I share with every group I bring here.
Where is the Ziggurat of Ur?

The ruins of Ur lie at Tell al-Muqayyar, which means "the mound of bitumen", in Dhi Qar province. The site is about 15 km southwest of the city of Nasiriyah, on a wide, flat plain west of the Euphrates. In ancient times the river and the marshy shore of the Gulf were much closer, and Ur was a busy port and trading city. Over the centuries the river changed its course, the land dried out, and the city was finally abandoned around the 4th century BC.
Today the ziggurat appears on the horizon long before you reach it: a huge block of golden-brown brick rising out of the desert, with nothing around it but sky. It is one of those places where the scale of the landscape makes the monument feel even bigger.
The history of the Great Ziggurat of Ur

Built by King Ur-Nammu around 2100 BC:
The ziggurat was begun around 2100 BC by King Ur-Nammu, the founder of the Third Dynasty of Ur, a time when Ur was the capital of a powerful Sumerian state. The work was completed by his son, King Shulgi. Many of the baked bricks are still stamped with Ur-Nammu's name, a royal signature you can sometimes spot in the walls.
A stairway to the moon god:
A ziggurat is not a tomb and not a pyramid. It is a raised temple platform, built in stages, with a shrine on the very top. The Ziggurat of Ur was dedicated to Nanna, the Sumerian moon god (known as Sin in Akkadian), the patron of the city. Priests climbed the staircases to the sanctuary at the summit, closer to the sky, while the city spread out below around its temples, palaces and houses.
Restored by Nabonidus:
Some 1,500 years after Ur-Nammu, the ziggurat had crumbled. In the 6th century BC the Neo-Babylonian king Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon and a devoted follower of the moon god, restored it. His inscribed clay cylinders, placed in the corners of the building, were found by explorers in the 1850s and helped identify the site as ancient Ur.
Rediscovered by archaeologists:
The mound was described by William Loftus in 1850, but Ur became world famous thanks to Sir Leonard Woolley, who led a joint expedition of the British Museum and the Penn Museum from 1922 to 1934. His team uncovered the ziggurat, the temple quarter, residential streets and the spectacular Royal Cemetery. In the 1980s the façade of the lowest stage and the great front staircase were partially reconstructed, which is why the lower part looks so sharp and complete today.
What to see at the ziggurat

The massive base:
The base measures roughly 64 by 45 metres. Archaeologists estimate the original height at more than 30 metres, although only the lower parts survive. The core is solid mud brick, wrapped in a thick skin of baked brick set in bitumen, the natural asphalt that gave the site its Arabic name.
Three monumental staircases:
The front of the ziggurat is defined by three great stairways: one in the centre and two running along the façade, all meeting at a gateway on the first terrace. Standing at the foot of the central stair and looking up is the classic moment of any visit.
Clever ancient engineering:
Look closely at the walls and you will notice narrow vertical slots. These "weeper holes" let moisture escape from the mud-brick core, so the building would not crack from the inside. Woolley also noticed that the walls lean slightly inwards and that the lines are gently curved, a trick that makes the structure look even more powerful from below.
More to explore in ancient Ur

The Royal Cemetery:
Next to the temple area lies the Royal Cemetery, where Woolley's team found the tombs of Sumerian kings and queens, including Queen Puabi. Their treasures, such as the Standard of Ur, the Great Lyre and the famous "Ram in a Thicket", are today shared between the Iraq Museum in Baghdad, the British Museum and the Penn Museum. On site you can see the shafts and brick chambers where they were discovered.
Enheduanna and the house of the high priestess:
Ur was also home to Enheduanna, daughter of King Sargon of Akkad, who served as high priestess of Nanna here around the 23rd century BC. She wrote hymns to the gods and is the first author in history known to us by name. The remains of the giparu, the residence of the high priestesses, lie close to the ziggurat.
The House of Abraham:
In the old residential quarter, among streets of Old Babylonian houses, one restored building is traditionally called the House of Abraham. According to tradition, the Prophet Abraham was born in Ur of the Chaldees, and for Jewish, Christian and Muslim visitors alike this gives the site a special, reflective atmosphere. Nearby are the brick mausolea of the kings Shulgi and Amar-Sin.
Since 2016 Ur has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site "The Ahwar of Southern Iraq", together with Uruk, Eridu and the Mesopotamian Marshes.
How to get to Ur from Baghdad

Ur is in the far south, so most travellers visit it on a multi-day trip. From Baghdad to Nasiriyah it is around 360 km by road, roughly five hours depending on stops. From Nasiriyah the site is a short drive. From Basra the journey takes around two to two and a half hours. The most rewarding plan is to sleep in Nasiriyah and combine Ur with the Mesopotamian Marshes at Chibayish and with Basra and Qurna. Allow at least two hours for the ziggurat, the Royal Cemetery and the House of Abraham.
Best time to visit the Ziggurat of Ur

The best season is from October to April, when days are warm and sunny but comfortable. Summers in southern Iraq are extremely hot, and there is almost no shade on the site. Come early in the morning or in the late afternoon: the low sun turns the bricks deep gold against a clear blue sky, and the photographs are at their best.
Practical tips for visiting Ur

• Bring plenty of water, a hat and sunscreen; there is little shade and few facilities on the site.
• Wear sturdy, comfortable shoes for walking on uneven ground and brick paths.
• Rules about climbing the staircase can change, so always follow the instructions of the site guards.
• Do not take bricks or pottery shards, however small; everything on the site is protected heritage.
• Combine Ur with a visit to the Iraq Museum in Baghdad to see the treasures found here.
• Entry rules for Iraq change from time to time, so check the latest official visa information before you book.
Every time I bring guests to Ur, there is a moment of silence when they reach the foot of the great staircase. Then someone always asks: "Abraham walked here?" I tell them the story, we look up at the ziggurat against the blue sky, and we feel how deep the roots of this land go. — Saif
The Ziggurat of Ur on an Iraq tour

Ur is one of the highlights of our 7-day Iraq tour, together with the Marshes and the great Mesopotamian sites further north. If you love ancient history, read our guide to visiting Babylon and the story of the Ishtar Gate. Seeing Babylon and Ur on the same journey is the best way to understand how Mesopotamia shaped the world: from the first cities and the first writing to the temples where people once looked up to the moon.

q: Where is the Malwiya minaret?
In Samarra, Salah al-Din province, on the east bank of the Tigris about 125 km north of Baghdad, next to the walls of the Great Mosque of Samarra.
Who built the spiral minaret of Samarra?
The Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil built it between 848 and 852 together with the Great Mosque, when Samarra was the capital of the caliphate.
How tall is the Malwiya?
It is about 52 metres high and roughly 33 metres wide at the base, with a spiral ramp winding around the outside up to a small pavilion at the top.
Can you climb the Malwiya minaret?
Climbing is not always permitted; access is decided on site by the staff. If it is allowed, wear good shoes, because the ramp has no railing.
How do I get to Samarra from Baghdad?
Samarra is about 125 km north of Baghdad, roughly two hours by road, and makes an easy day trip with a driver and guide.
What else can I see in Samarra?
The Great Mosque walls, the Abu Dulaf Mosque with a smaller spiral minaret, remains of the Abbasid palaces and the al-Askari shrine with its golden dome.
s: The Malwiya minaret of Samarra: history, what to see and how to visit

Few buildings in the Islamic world are as easy to recognise as the Malwiya minaret of Samarra. A tower of golden-brown brick winds upwards in a wide spiral, like a giant seashell standing on the plain beside the Tigris. Visiting the Malwiya minaret in Samarra means standing at the foot of a monument raised more than 1,170 years ago, when this city was the capital of the Abbasid caliphs and one of the largest cities of its time.
In this guide I explain where Samarra is, why the caliphs built a capital here, what makes the spiral minaret and the Great Mosque so special, what else to see in the city, and how to fit Samarra into a journey through Iraq.
Where is the Malwiya minaret?

Samarra lies on the east bank of the Tigris in Salah al-Din province, about 125 km north of Baghdad. By road the drive usually takes roughly two hours depending on traffic, through farmland, palm groves and open steppe. The minaret stands at the northern edge of the modern town, next to the vast brick walls of the Great Mosque of Samarra, and you can see its spiral long before you arrive.
The whole area belongs to the Samarra Archaeological City, which UNESCO added to its World Heritage List in 2007. The ancient city stretched for kilometres along the river, with palaces, mosques, racecourses and gardens, and much of it still lies under the sand as low mounds and outlines.
Samarra, the short-lived capital of the Abbasids

A new city on the Tigris:
In 836 the Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tasim moved his court away from Baghdad and founded a new capital at Samarra. Its full name is often explained as Surra man ra'a, "a joy for whoever sees it". For more than half a century, until 892, the caliphs ruled from here, and they filled the city with monumental buildings on a scale that still impresses archaeologists today.
Al-Mutawakkil, the great builder:
The caliph who left the strongest mark on Samarra was al-Mutawakkil. Between 848 and 851 he built the Great Mosque, and between 848 and 852 its famous minaret. A few years later, around 859, he added a second large mosque north of the city, today called the Abu Dulaf Mosque. When the caliphs returned to Baghdad, Samarra slowly became a quiet provincial town, which is one reason why so much of its 9th-century layout survived.
The spiral minaret: how it works

The Malwiya is about 52 metres high and roughly 33 metres wide at its base. Its name comes from the Arabic word for "twisted" or "coiled", and many people describe it as a snail shell. A broad ramp runs around the outside of the tower, getting narrower as it climbs, until it reaches a small round pavilion at the top with arched openings.
There is no staircase inside: the spiral ramp is the only way up. The tower was built of brick on a square base and originally stood just outside the mosque, joined to it by a bridge. Scholars still discuss why the architects chose this shape. Some see a memory of the old Mesopotamian ziggurats, the stepped temple towers you can still visit at Ur and near Babylon. Others see a bold statement of the caliph's power, a landmark visible from far across the plain. Either way, nothing quite like it had been built before.
Every time I bring guests to Samarra, the first moment is always the same: the bus stops, everyone looks up, and nobody says a word for a few seconds. In the late afternoon the bricks turn the colour of honey against a deep blue sky. It is my favourite photo stop in all of Iraq. — Saif, your guide
The Great Mosque of Samarra

Once the largest mosque in the world:
When it was completed in 851, the Great Mosque of Samarra was the largest mosque in the world. Its outer enclosure covered more than 16 hectares, and historians estimate that it could hold more than 60,000 worshippers. Today you can walk along its massive baked-brick walls, strengthened by 44 semicircular towers, and step through the gateways into the huge open courtyard.
What it looked like inside:
Only the outer walls and the minaret have survived, so imagination helps. Sources describe a prayer hall with 17 aisles, 464 pillars, ceilings around 11 metres high and walls decorated with dark blue glass mosaics. Standing in the empty courtyard and picturing that forest of columns gives you a real sense of the scale of Abbasid ambition.
A model for Cairo:
The Samarra mosque inspired builders far beyond Iraq. The Mosque of Ibn Tulun in Cairo, built a few decades later, followed it in many respects and even has its own minaret with an outside staircase. If you have visited Cairo, you will recognise the family resemblance immediately.
More to see in Samarra

• The Abu Dulaf Mosque: about 15 km north of the city, built by al-Mutawakkil around 859. Its spiral minaret is smaller, about 32 metres, and the site is usually much quieter.
• Remains of the caliphal palaces: brick arches and courtyards that hint at the size of the Abbasid court.
• The al-Askari shrine: one of the most important holy shrines in Iraq, with a shining golden dome, visited by pilgrims from many countries. It is a place of prayer, so visitors dress modestly and follow the guidance of the shrine staff.
Best time to visit Samarra

The most pleasant months are from October to April, when days are mild and the sky is often clear. Summer in central Iraq is extremely hot, so if you travel then, plan the visit for early morning or late afternoon. For photography, the hour before sunset is ideal: the spiral throws long shadows and the brick glows warm and golden.
Practical tips for your visit

• Climbing the spiral ramp is not always permitted; access is decided on site, so please follow the instructions of the site staff.
• If climbing is allowed, wear shoes with good grip: the ramp has no railing and becomes narrow near the top.
• Bring a hat, sunglasses and water. There is very little shade around the mosque walls.
• Allow at least one to two hours for the minaret and the Great Mosque, more if you add Abu Dulaf.
• When visiting the al-Askari shrine, women should bring a headscarf and long loose clothing; men should wear long trousers.
• Entry rules for Iraq change from time to time, so check the current visa requirements for your nationality before you book.
Samarra on an Iraq tour

Samarra is an easy and rewarding day trip from Baghdad, and it fits perfectly into a heritage itinerary that also covers Babylon, the holy cities of Najaf and Karbala, and the Sumerian south. On our 7-day Iraq tour we combine the spiral minaret with the city's other Abbasid monuments, so you see the golden age of Islamic Mesopotamia right after the ancient world of Babylon and Ur. If you are also interested in early Islamic architecture, the Great Mosque of Kufa makes a fascinating comparison.
Whatever else you see in Iraq, the moment you stand beneath the Malwiya and follow its spiral up into the sky is one you will remember for a long time.
